name: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
title: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
answer: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review, often called TAR, are methods for finding relevant documents in large e-discovery collections by using machine learning to rank or classify documents. The scope covers civil litigation, regulatory investigations, and internal investigations where manual review of every document is impractical. TAR includes workflows based on initial seed sets and continuous active learning, where the system repeatedly proposes documents for human review. It is used for responsiveness, privilege, and issue coding across emails, contracts, chat, and other unstructured data.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review, often called TAR, are methods for finding relevant documents in large e-discovery collections by using machine learning to rank or classify documents. The scope covers civil litigation, regulatory investigations, and internal investigations where manual review of every document is impractical. TAR includes workflows based on initial seed sets and continuous active learning, where the system repeatedly proposes documents for human review. It is used for responsiveness, privilege, and issue coding across emails, contracts, chat, and other unstructured data.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: TAR runs on e-discovery platforms that store processed text and metadata, typically in cloud or on-premises data centers. The infrastructure requires indexed text, optical character recognition for scanned documents, and pipelines that extract native files into reviewable form. Compute needs are modest compared to large language models, and many workflows operate on standard servers or cloud instances. The human review interface, with coding panels and batch assignments, is a core part of the technical setup.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through an iterative loop in which subject matter experts label a sample of documents, the system learns from those labels, ranks the remaining population, and additional high-value documents are reviewed and labeled to improve the model. In continuous active learning, the system selects the next document most likely to be relevant for human review, rather than relying on random samples. Quality is measured with recall, precision, and elusion tests, often using control sets that are not used for training.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance center on defensibility, transparency, and privilege. Parties typically negotiate a protocol for using TAR, including how training documents, seed sets, and validation metrics will be handled. Courts have accepted TAR when the process is documented and reasonable, but disputes arise over disclosure of non-responsive training documents and over whether the requesting party can inspect the model. Privilege review remains a human responsibility, and errors can lead to sanctions if production is incomplete. Provenance requires audit logs of coding decisions, model versions, and review history.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: TAR is merging with generative AI and large language models to draft privilege logs, summarize document clusters, and propose relevance rationales. Active learning is becoming more integrated with continuous review workflows and with tools that identify important documents earlier in a matter. The focus is shifting from binary relevance to issue coding, sentiment, and fact extraction across mixed media, including chat, audio, and video. Courts and rules committees are likely to address validation standards for these newer methods.
